paragraphs.heading: Putting a date on the past
paragraphs.text: Chronological dating, or simply dating, means giving an object or event a date in the past so it can be placed in a chronology that is already worked out. This usually needs what is called a dating method. Many fields use such methods, among them history, geology, paleontology, archaeology, astronomy and even forensic science, where investigators sometimes have to find out when a death took place.

paragraphs.heading: Relative and absolute
paragraphs.text: Dating methods are most often sorted into two groups. Absolute dating gives a specific date or a range of dates. Relative dating instead places things on a timeline compared with other events or objects. A relative method cannot tell you an object's actual age, but it can show that an event could not have happened before, or after, another event whose date is well known.

paragraphs.heading: Shakespeare and the year 1587
paragraphs.text: Historians use this reasoning with Shakespeare's play Henry V. Shakespeare drew mainly on Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles, in its second edition, and that edition did not appear until 1587. So the play was certainly written after 1587, which makes 1587 its post quem date. The Latin terms post quem and ante quem mark the oldest and the most recent possible moments for an event.

paragraphs.heading: Pollen as a time marker
paragraphs.text: Archaeology, geology and paleontology apply the same kind of reasoning in many ways. When a layer, or stratum, is hard to date absolutely, scientists can study the fossil pollen inside it, a field called paleopalynology. This works because some plant species, whether extinct or not, are known to belong to a definite position on the time scale.

paragraphs.heading: Absolute dates
paragraphs.text: Absolute methods try to pin down the specific time when an object came into being or an event happened. They rely mainly on radiometric dating. Scientists largely accept their results, though sampling errors and geological disruptions can stand in the way of an accurate date. Radiocarbon dating, also called carbon dating, can reveal the age of organic material in artifacts and in human and animal remains, reliably back to about 50,000 years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Dating a church from its bricks
paragraphs.text: Thermoluminescence (TL) dating can show roughly how many years ago a piece of brick was fired. It was used on bricks taken from St. James Church in Toruń, and the date it gave filled a gap in what was known about the church's history. Geologists, too, apply absolute methods to rock sediment to find out when it formed.

paragraphs.heading: From ancient caves to recent finds
paragraphs.text: The span covered by archaeological dating can be huge. Caves at Pinnacle Point, on the southern coast of South Africa, show that humans were regularly gathering shellfish as of 170,000 years ago. Yet remains only about a hundred years old can be dated as well, as with an 18th-century sloop excavated in South Carolina in 1992.
